name: Quarkus (Vert.x/Netty, JDK 21)
baseline: nginx (C, hand-written handler module compiled -O3 -march=native, per HttpArena frameworks.json) in the HttpArena suite; h2o, Drogon, Mongoose, libreactorng and other C/C++ rows come from the same results directory
workload: HttpArena request throughput on one 64-core machine (mixed GET/POST with query parsing at 4096 connections, plus pipelined, HTTP/2 and h2c baseline profiles as listed). Entry is Quarkus with RESTEasy Reactive on Vert.x/Netty, JDK 21, 'optimized JVM tuning' (HttpArena tuned mode).
claimed_speedup: baseline-h2c-256: 6,188,551 req/s vs nginx 2,456,329 (2.52x, derived from page data); baseline-h2-256: 4,668,449 req/s vs nginx 3,414,750 (1.37x, derived from page data), h2o 16,106,978 (0.29x); pipelined-4096: 7,858,636 req/s vs nginx 4,037,345 (1.95x, derived from page data), h2o 4,938,603 (1.59x), drogon 7,801,404 (1.01x); baseline-4096: 1,818,132 req/s vs nginx 3,284,513 (0.55x, derived from page data), h2o 3,641,609 (0.50x), drogon 2,022,710 (0.90x)
compiler_and_flags: JDK 21 with optimized JVM tuning flags (HttpArena frameworks/quarkus-jvm); JIT, not matched to nginx -O3
hardware: HttpArena dedicated 64-core machine, one container per entry (README: '64-core dedicated hardware'); CPU model, RAM, NIC and kernel not stated
tradeoffs: JVM start-up and warm-up cost and memory footprint are not part of the throughput figure; Netty/Vert.x event loop under a full framework.
caveats: Beats nginx only on HTTP/2 profiles and pipelining; at baseline-4096 it is 0.55x of nginx (1,818,132 vs 3,284,513) and 0.90x of Drogon, and 0.29x of h2o at baseline-h2-256. HttpArena results JSON files are undated and the suite is rerun by its maintainers; competitor rows were read from sibling JSON files in the same directory (nginx.json, h2o.json, drogon.json). The nginx entry is a custom C handler module, not a stock config, and every entry is a minimal hand-written handler, so this measures server-engine overhead on a mixed GET/POST baseline workload, not static-file serving. CPU model is not stated, so the entry cannot be tier A. The pipelined profile is marked reference-only in the HttpArena README (excluded from its composite score), and nginx's h2 and h2c rows sit far below h2o's, so wins over nginx there say little about h2o.
found_via: HttpArena leaderboard data (github.com/MDA2AV/HttpArena site/data/frameworks.json and site/data/results/<name>.json via raw.githubusercontent.com), mined for registry-listed servers after the crates.io searches 'http server', 'io_uring http' and 'reverse proxy' surfaced the Rust io_uring and tokio ecosystems
why_faster: Netty event loops under Vert.x with JVM tuning (HttpArena description); no mechanism is given for the h2c gap to nginx.

name: Undertow
baseline: nginx (echo module) plus Kore, libmicrohttpd, Onion (C) and Crow (C++) in the same table
workload: Trivial dynamic 'Hello World' text/plain response over HTTP/1.1 keep-alive with wrk, 100 connections, framework overhead only (no database, no JSON).
claimed_speedup: 616,547 req/s (3.29 ms p99) vs Kore 572,782 (1.08x, derived from page data), libmicrohttpd 533,626 (1.16x), Onion 483,824 (1.27x), nginx with echo module 381,368 (1.62x), Crow 256,552 (2.40x).
compiler_and_flags: JVM and Undertow versions not stated; Kore built with 'make NOTLS=1'; other C/C++ flags not stated
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-1650 @ 3.50GHz, 32 GB RAM, Ubuntu 14.04 LTS, Linux 3.16; load generator wrk run on the same machine (time.sh: -c100, four 20 s runs, 10 s warm-up)
tradeoffs: JVM start-up, warm-up and memory are not part of the throughput figure; larger footprint than the C servers in the table.
caveats: Benchmark is from about November 2015 (response header sample dated 24 Nov 2015) and library versions are not stated, so it is far older than current Undertow, Netty, Kore, libmicrohttpd, Onion, Crow and nginx. The suite is a single-author repo (53 stars) that re-runs TechEmpower-style hello-world on one machine with the load generator on the same host; wrk thread count is not in the README (default set in common/threads.sh). Compiler flags for the C and C++ servers are not stated (only Kore is noted as built with 'make NOTLS=1'); the nginx row uses the echo module and is not a tuned static config; frameworks add different header sets so bytes per response differ. The Undertow README itself carries no benchmark numbers.
found_via: WebSearch 'Java HTTP server benchmark outperforms nginx wrk requests per second github README' surfaced a nanoant/WebFrameworkBenchmark commit; README table opened on github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com
why_faster: The suite's conclusion only says Undertow 'is most optimized'; no mechanism is given.

name: Netty
baseline: nginx (echo module) and Crow (C++) in the same table
workload: Trivial dynamic 'Hello World' text/plain response over HTTP/1.1 keep-alive with wrk, 100 connections, framework overhead only.
claimed_speedup: 422,580 req/s (4.08 ms p99) vs nginx with echo module 381,368 (1.11x, derived from page data) and Crow 256,552 (1.65x); behind Kore 572,782, libmicrohttpd 533,626 and Onion 483,824.
compiler_and_flags: JVM and Netty versions not stated; C/C++ flags not stated
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-1650 @ 3.50GHz, 32 GB RAM, Ubuntu 14.04 LTS, Linux 3.16; load generator wrk run on the same machine (time.sh: -c100, four 20 s runs, 10 s warm-up)
tradeoffs: JVM start-up, warm-up and memory are not part of the throughput figure; Netty is a networking toolkit, so the benchmarked server is hand-written on top of it.
caveats: Benchmark is from about November 2015 (response header sample dated 24 Nov 2015) and library versions are not stated, so it is far older than current Undertow, Netty, Kore, libmicrohttpd, Onion, Crow and nginx. The suite is a single-author repo (53 stars) that re-runs TechEmpower-style hello-world on one machine with the load generator on the same host; wrk thread count is not in the README (default set in common/threads.sh). Compiler flags for the C and C++ servers are not stated (only Kore is noted as built with 'make NOTLS=1'); the nginx row uses the echo module and is not a tuned static config; frameworks add different header sets so bytes per response differ. Netty loses to all three C servers in the same table, so the claim is only against nginx's echo module and Crow.
found_via: WebSearch 'Java HTTP server benchmark outperforms nginx wrk requests per second github README' surfaced a nanoant/WebFrameworkBenchmark commit; README table opened on github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com

name: cblt
workload: Apache Benchmark, 3000 requests at 1000 concurrent connections, downloading a 23 KB logo.png from 127.0.0.1; response-time percentiles.
claimed_speedup: Percentile table (units not stated, ab reports ms): 50%: 179 vs nginx 1209 (6.75x lower, derived from page data); 75%: 194 vs 1655 (8.53x); 100%: 200 vs 2146 (10.73x). README feature list: '10 times faster than Nginx for small content under 100KB'.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (Cargo.toml: tokio, httparse, rustls, async-compression); nginx from the nginx:latest image
tradeoffs: Minimal file server and reverse proxy with load balancing, Docker label integration and TLS; far fewer features than nginx.
caveats: Single run of one 23 KB file; hardware, OS, ab flags beyond -c/-n, nginx config and the unit of the table are not stated; the '10x faster for content under 100KB' headline is supported by one file only. The repo has benchmark/ab.md (ab -c 100 -n 300 on logo_huge.png) with no numbers. A percentile table at 1000 connections for 3000 requests mostly reflects connection queueing, not steady-state throughput. Last commit June 2025.
found_via: WebSearch 'Rust web server benchmark faster than nginx wrk requests per second static files' and crates.io API search q='faster than nginx' (cblt: 'Safe and fast minimalistic web server, written in Rust')

name: Spire
baseline: HAProxy 2.7.3 (C) and Envoy 1.22.8 (C++) reverse proxies; nginx 1.23.3 in the same table is faster than Spire
workload: hey -n 100000 -c 250 GET through each reverse proxy to one backend, docker-compose, proxy and backend limited to 4 CPU cores and 8 GB memory; based on the public NickMRamirez/Proxy-Benchmarks harness.
claimed_speedup: Spire 114,512 req/s (avg 2.2 ms, p99 11.8 ms) vs HAProxy 85,406 (1.34x, derived from page data), Envoy 48,040 (2.38x), Traefik 59,487 (1.93x), Caddy 13,168 (8.70x); but nginx 1.23.3 reached 148,677 req/s, so Spire is 0.77x of nginx (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated; proxies run as Docker images in docker-compose (versions listed: HAProxy 2.7.3, Envoy 1.22.8, Traefik 2.9.8, NGINX 1.23.3, Caddy 2.6.4); Spire built with cargo build --release per README
hardware: 13th Gen Intel Core i5-13600K PC, 32 GB RAM (benchmarks.md); services limited to 4 cores and 8 GB
tradeoffs: Rust reverse proxy and gateway on Tokio and Hyper (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, gRPC, TCP/TLS) with rate limiting, circuit breaking, ACME and hot reload; about 7 MB binary and 4 MB start-up memory per README.
caveats: Not faster than nginx in its own table (114,512 vs 148,677 req/s, p99 11.8 ms vs 4.9 ms); the claim holds only against HAProxy, Envoy, Traefik and Caddy. Single hey run of 100,000 requests lasting about 1 s per proxy, load generator on the same PC, old HAProxy 2.7.3 and Envoy 1.22.8 releases, default or unstated proxy configs, and the README headline 'Exceptional Performance' is not backed by a win over nginx. Flags are not stated, so it cannot be tier A.
found_via: WebSearch 'Rust OR Go reverse proxy load balancer github benchmark outperforms nginx and HAProxy requests per second README' and github.com/topics/reverse-proxy?l=rust; README and benchmarks.md opened
why_faster: README attributes it to the Tokio async runtime and the Hyper HTTP library; no mechanism analysis is given.

name: Aralez
baseline: nginx (version and config not stated, 'tuned as much as I could'); Traefik (Go) in the same chart
workload: Reverse proxy in front of three nginx upstreams returning a hard-coded JSON body, 800 concurrent users, three batches: HTTP/1.1 plain-text endpoint, HTTP/2 over SSL, and a mixed HTTP/1.1 plus HTTP/2 workload; one server runs the proxies on different ports.
claimed_speedup: No numbers in the README text for the comparison; the result is a Grafana chart (assets/bench.png). Values read off the plot, approximate: Aralez about 107k, 78k and 87k req/s in the three batches vs nginx about 70-75k, 65-70k and 65-75k, Traefik about 58k, 36k and 43k. README text separately says Aralez alone reaches 107k-110k req/s (glibc build) and 97k-100k (musl build) in its most intensive tests.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the comparison; Aralez release binaries aralez-x86_64-glibc and musl builds; nginx build flags not stated
hardware: Intel Xeon E-2174G @ 3.80 GHz, 64 GB RAM, four servers on one 1 Gbit switch in a datacenter (README); the separate Aralez-only runs list a Xeon E3-1270 v6
tradeoffs: Rust reverse proxy and ingress-style load balancer built on Cloudflare's Pingora (already catalogued) with Consul and Kubernetes discovery, hot reload, automatic TLS and HTTP/2; the comparison therefore measures a Pingora-based proxy against nginx.
caveats: Comparison numbers exist only as a chart image (Grafana screenshot with no table), so the values above are approximate readings; nginx and Traefik versions and configs, the load generator and the exact duration are not stated for the comparison. The README says the figures reflect 'synthetic performance under optimal conditions'. Its text numbers (129,777 req/s with oha, 107k-110k req/s) come from Aralez-only runs on different hardware and are inconsistent with each other. HAProxy appears only in a feature table, not in any benchmark. The proxy is a layer on Pingora, so a verifier may fold it into the Pingora entry.
found_via: github.com/topics/reverse-proxy?l=rust listed sadoyan/aralez; README 'Aralez, Nginx, Traefik performance benchmark' section and assets/bench.png opened
why_faster: README credits the Pingora engine and Rust ('world-class performance'); no mechanism analysis versus nginx is given.
